caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:000055
attempts.paper_title: Behavioral and Neural Variability of Naturalistic Arm Movements
attempts.entry_title: Behavioral and neural variability of naturalistic arm movements (Peterson et al. 2021)
attempts.summary: The paper's main findings hold up in this data: at the onset of naturalistic arm movements, low-frequency power falls and high-frequency power rises, most in precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal cortex, and behavior and this power vary significantly across subjects and recording days. Regression models of single-event power explain little variance (largest withheld R2 0.189), with reach angle and recording day the most informative features. The per-subject event counts did not reproduce, likely because the files hold 8088 events with none marked as a false positive. Whether low-frequency decreases are more widespread could not be tested, as the paper does not say how this was measured. A few minor details, such as the reach angle peaks, partly differ.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Peterson, Singh, Wang, Rao and Brunton (2021) on dandiset 000055 (AJILE12), which holds 55 days of ECoG and pose from 12 people in clinical epilepsy monitoring, with their wrist movement events and event features. It compares the behavioural features across subjects and days, the group and per-subject movement-related spectral power in eight cortical regions, the variation of precentral band power across subjects and recording days, and the regression of single-event band power on the behavioural features (Figure 6).

notebooks.title: Reproducing Peterson et al. (2021) from dandiset 000055

outcomes.notes: The dataset's subjects 01 to 12 have exactly the days of Table 2, 55 subject-days in all, so subjects are matched by number. No two files share event times or wrist traces.

For all 12 subjects the rows used equal the electrodes of the NWB file. S01's matrix has 98 rows for 94 electrodes; the last four are all zero and are dropped by the code's rule. The all-zero rows of S03 (16) and S12 (8) fall on whole depth groups (LAD and LPD; AID). The region with the largest weight is the one with the nearest centroid for 0.587 to 0.786 of electrodes, against 0.163 to 0.258 with the electrode order shuffled, in all 12 subjects; the Spearman correlation of weight with proximity is 0.916 to 0.937. The regions with mean density above 3 are the eight the claims file names.
deviations: This link claim was written by the author during the attempt (protocol, author step 4), after the electrode and row counts had been listed.

outcomes.notes: No value is recorded under measured, as two of the seven expected values (male subjects, mean age) cannot be measured. 12 subjects, a mean of 84.8 surface electrodes (SD 11.6; 87.0 +- 12.9), a mean of 23.7 depth electrodes in the subjects with depth electrodes (23.2 +- 12.1) and 5 subjects implanted in the right hemisphere (judged by the wrist of the events, which agrees with the sign of the mean MNI x) match. Seven subjects (S01, S02, S03, S09, S10, S11, S12) have electrode groups whose description says depth, where the paper says five. Sex and age are not in the files or the archive's metadata and are not testable. The data descriptor of the dataset (doi 10.1038/s41597-022-01280-y, Table 2) counts S10 as 86 surface and 40 depth electrodes and S11 as 106 surface and none, where the group descriptions give 78 and 48, and 88 and 18. With the descriptor's counts the surface mean is 87.0 +- 12.9 and six subjects have depth electrodes (23.3 +- 12.0), so the count of five fails under both. The descriptor's table also lists sex and age (8 male, 4 female; ages with mean 29.4), which match the paper, but it is not the dataset and is not used for the outcome.
deviations: Depth electrodes are those in groups whose description in the file contains "depth"; the paper's per-subject table (Extended Data Figure 1-1) could not be read.

outcomes.notes: Reading a (all events) gives 211 to 996 events per subject, median 770.5; reading b (bad segments dropped) 211 to 979, median 739. The most is within tolerance under both; the fewest (against 151 +- 15.1) and the median (against 640 +- 64) are not. The files hold 8088 events and the data descriptor of the dataset states 6931 verified events. No event is marked as a false positive, and the paper removed 17.8% of events as false positives or occlusions, so the dataset likely holds events the paper dropped. The reaches table has the same nine columns in all 55 files and none marks false positives or verified events, so the outcome rests on reading a in full and on reading b without its false-positive step. The reading b median less 14% (739 x 0.86 = 636) would lie within tolerance, so the shortfall may come from the missing marks.
deviations: The false-positive removal of reading b cannot be applied, as the files do not mark false positives.

The bad-segment rule of reading b uses an assumed summary of segment power (see fig3-group-lfb-decrease-hfb-increase); here it drops 1 segment below 0 dB, 74 with high 115-125 Hz power and 124 with missing samples.

outcomes.notes: All ten Kruskal-Wallis tests across the 12 subjects give p < 0.001 under reading b (7888 events) and reading a (8088); the largest p is 9.9e-35 (reach duration).
deviations: Reach angle is the files' angle negated and folded onto -90 to 90 degrees. The files store the angle in image coordinates (it matches the wrist trace to a median of 1.46 degrees, and to 116.58 degrees when negated), and the code negates it and folds 90-270 degrees. Time of day is in hours from the files' midnight clock.

outcomes.notes: Duration and magnitude part holds. Pooled, 0.918 of reaches last under 2 s and 0.915 cover under 200 pixels, and both shares exceed one half in all 12 subjects (lowest 0.881 and 0.591, S08 for magnitude). Angle part does not hold. The two highest maxima of the angle density lie at -71.5 and 75.0 degrees pooled and within 15 degrees of +-90 in no subject; S02 and S04 have a single maximum, and in S03, S06 and S07 the density at 0 exceeds the lower peak. 22.9% of reaches lie within 30 degrees of horizontal. Reading a gives the same. The criterion's KDE has no boundary correction, and on synthetic angles whose density peaks at +-90 it puts the peaks at -72.5 and 70.0 (n = 250) and -73.5 and 74.0 degrees (n = 900), so the criterion is biased against the angle part. With the data reflected at +-90 (a sensitivity output, not the criterion) the peaks lie within 15 degrees of +-90 pooled and in 6 of 12 subjects, still not more than half, so the outcome is the same. Asked of a reader (questions/000055.yaml).
deviations: Angle convention as in fig2-features-differ-across-subjects.

outcomes.notes: The median bimanual ratio is below 0.5 (pooled 0.136) and the overlap skewness positive (pooled 1.114) in all 12 subjects; the class is bimanual for 0.725 of events pooled and more than half in all 12 (lowest 0.507, S12). The five highest median ratios are S04, S07, S05, S02, S03 and the five lowest overlap skewness S07, S05, S02, S03, S04, so S02, S04 and S05 are in both. Reading a gives the same.
deviations: Bimanual ratio has no missing values in the files (26 events are exactly 0.5), so the code's fill of 0.5 changes nothing.

outcomes.notes: The peak over 0 to 1.5 s of the median contralateral displacement exceeds the ipsilateral one in all 12 subjects under reading a (rest position the mean over -1.5 to -1 s; ratios 1.12 to 37.81, median 4.3) and reading b (position at onset; ratios 1.08 to 42.01, median 5.83). The margin is small for S04 (1.12 and 1.32) and S05 (1.15 and 1.08), so "substantially" holds for 10 of 12 subjects if read as a ratio above 1.5.

Five of six pooled Pearson correlations are within tolerance under reading b; reach magnitude and duration give 0.233 against 0.26 +- 0.026 (lower bound 0.234). Reading a gives 0.231, 0.609, 0.505, 0.501, 0.494 and 0.598, also five of six.

The busiest day holds more than half of the events for S05 (0.605) and S09 (0.517) and for none of the other subjects, but S04's busiest day holds 0.379, so the day part does not hold as written. More than half of each subject's events fall at 08 to 24 h (0.641 to 0.964), so the waking part holds. Reading a gives the same.
deviations: The hour of an event is taken from the files' clock, which starts at midnight; the Sleep/rest labels fall mostly in its first hours (0.545 of them at 0 to 8 h).

outcomes.notes: After the bootstrap mask, the mean over 4-30 Hz and 0 to 0.5 s is negative and over 50-120 Hz positive in precentral (-0.885 and 0.496 dB), postcentral (-0.890 and 0.507) and inferior parietal (-0.663 and 0.277), and also at the onset time bin (-0.748 and 0.460, -0.742 and 0.477, -0.592 and 0.278). Middle frontal, supramarginal and middle temporal (-0.005 and 0.003 dB) show the same pattern over 0 to 0.5 s; at the onset bin supramarginal's high-frequency value and middle temporal's low-frequency value are 0.000.
deviations: Region power uses the paper's projection matrices from Figshare (claim roi-projection-link), not a new projection from the AAL atlas.

The bad electrodes are those of each subject's first file, as the code takes them (tfr_utils.py, load_project_spectral_power, which reads info['bads'] from the first power file of each subject only); the files' good flags differ between days for every subject.

Assumed reading of the bad-segment rule (Methods, "discarding segments with power <0 dB or with abnormally high power at 115-125 Hz (>3 SDs) compared with all segments"). The paper's preprocessing code is not published. The segment's Welch power density in microvolts squared per Hz is averaged over 1-200 Hz (or 115-125 Hz), converted to dB and averaged over good electrodes; the 3 SD limit is taken over the subject's segments. Averaging the log density instead would drop 7931 of 8087 segments, so that reading is not usable. Segments with missing samples are dropped (Methods, "segments with missing data").
The bootstrap mask covers -4.5 to 4.5 s (the 10 s segment less the code's 0.5 s pad), so the FDR correction runs over 25 x 91 bins per region; the paper's power files may span a different time range.
ECoG times in three files (S01 day 7, S04 day 3, S06 day 3) are shifted by 29241 to 30682 s, the ECoG missing at the start of the day (see findings).

The events include the false positives the paper removed (Methods, 17.8% of events removed as false positives or occlusions), as the files do not mark them (fig2-event-counts). This holds for every ECoG claim that refers to this one.

outcomes.notes: Under readings a, b and c postcentral, precentral and inferior parietal are the three largest regions and the temporal regions are below all three. Reading a gives 0.523, 0.512 and 0.336 dB, then middle frontal 0.236, supramarginal 0.093 and the temporal regions at most 0.039.
deviations: As for fig3-group-lfb-decrease-hfb-increase.

outcomes.notes: The criterion's two readings disagree, and the criterion blocks the claim when they do. Reading a counts 7 regions with a significant 4-30 Hz decrease and 7 with a significant 50-120 Hz increase over 0 to 0.5 s, so low frequencies are not more widespread. Reading b gives 35.2 significant decreasing bins per low frequency against 25.9 increasing bins per high frequency, so they are. Supramarginal (30 bins) and superior temporal (24 bins) both have significant low-frequency decreases; superior temporal has no significant high-frequency increase. Question for the paper's authors. How was "more spatially widespread" judged, as the number of regions with any significant change or as the extent of significant time-frequency bins? The Results sentence (Intracortical spectral power, paragraph 2) and Figure 3 give no measure; with region counts the two bands tie here at 7 of 8. The tie does not depend on the bootstrap seed. With ten other seeds reading a gives 7 against 7 regions every time and reading b 35.0 to 35.6 against 25.5 to 25.8 bins per frequency, and middle and inferior temporal keep 3 to 4 and 6 to 9 significant high-frequency bins.

All four parts hold. (1) Every subject has a negative 8-32 Hz mean and a positive 76-100 Hz mean in precentral over 0 to 0.5 s. (2) S03, S06, S07, S08 and S11 are positive at 116 and 121 Hz. (3) S09 and S12 both peak at 66 Hz among 56-121 Hz, with the 101-121 Hz mean (0.05 and 0.045 dB) below half the peak (0.373 and 0.289). (4) S08 has the narrowest decrease (2 bins); S03, S04, S05 and S07 tie at 3 bins for the next places, and by the interpolated width S08 (9.4 Hz), S04 (14.4 Hz) and S11 (16.8 Hz) are the three narrowest.
deviations: The bin count of part 4 ties four subjects for the second and third places. The tie is broken by the width in Hz of the run below half the minimum, interpolated between bins, a finer form of the same measure; the paper and its code give no rule. Under the bin count with the tie read against S04, part 4 fails and the claim would be partially reproduced. The interpolated width is also close for the third place (S11 16.8 Hz against S05 16.9 Hz), but S04 (14.4 Hz) is second.
As for fig3-group-lfb-decrease-hfb-increase.

outcomes.notes: Kruskal-Wallis across the 12 subjects (7888 events) gives p = 1.31e-163 for LFB and 7.06e-264 for HFB with the band mean, and 9.09e-165 and 7.79e-258 with the code's band median. With only segments with missing samples dropped (7963 events), p = 1.46e-165 and 7.68e-263.
deviations: As for fig3-group-lfb-decrease-hfb-increase, except that the outcome does not depend on the assumed bad-segment rule.

outcomes.notes: Under the reading mean over events of the band mean, 23 of 24 subject and band values lie inside the paper's intervals; S06 HFB is 1.782 dB against 2.02 to 2.37 (the bootstrap interval here is 1.64 to 1.92). The other readings give 21 (median of band mean), 21 (mean of band median) and 20 (median of band median) of 24. LFB is below baseline and HFB above it in all 12 subjects. With only segments with missing samples dropped, 22 of 24 (LFB 12, HFB 10).
deviations: As for fig3-group-lfb-decrease-hfb-increase; the outcome does not depend on the assumed bad-segment rule.

outcomes.notes: With the band mean, the per-subject Kruskal-Wallis tests across days agree with the paper on all 24 subject and band pairs, the 11 the paper names significant (largest p 0.0331, HFB S07) and the 13 others not (smallest p 0.068, HFB S01). With the code's band median, 23 of 24 agree; LFB S05 gives p = 0.088. With only segments with missing samples dropped, the same 11 pairs are significant.
deviations: As for fig5-band-power-differs-across-subjects.

outcomes.notes: Reading a (precentral region per subject), the SD across days of the day means is lower with baseline subtraction for 9 of 12 subjects in LFB (median 0.202 against 0.865 dB) and 12 of 12 in HFB (0.140 against 0.480 dB). Reading b (per good electrode), for 1006 of 1096 electrodes in LFB and 988 of 1096 in HFB. Variability remains, as 11 subject and band pairs have significant day effects after baseline subtraction (fig5-recording-day-effects).
deviations: As for fig3-group-lfb-decrease-hfb-increase. Power without baseline is the 10*log10 band power with no subtraction, with the data in microvolts.

outcomes.notes: The largest deviation of a day mean from the subject's mean precentral band power is 1.011 dB (S03 LFB), within 2.2 dB; the range of day means, the other reading the claims file mentions, reaches 1.801 dB. Without baseline subtraction the mean band power is 12.4 to 36.3 dB with the data in microvolts, inside 9 to 55 dB; in volts it would be -107.5 to -83.7 dB.
deviations: As for fig3-group-lfb-decrease-hfb-increase. The files store microvolts (conversion 1e-6 to volts), and the level part holds with that unit.

outcomes.notes: The largest split-averaged full-model withheld R2 over the 1096 good electrodes of the 12 subjects and both bands is 0.189 (HFB, S04), within 0.275; the largest in LFB is 0.149 (S01). The code's 80/20 split gives 0.192, the code's band median 0.203, and bad electrodes included 0.189. The median R2 is -0.014 in both bands, and 22 (LFB) and 14 (HFB) good electrodes exceed 0.05. For reference only, the R2 stored in the files reach 0.149 and 0.255; their Spearman correlation with the R2 here is 0.718 (LFB) and 0.643 (HFB) over 1088 good electrodes.
deviations: The Huber fits minimise the objective of sklearn's HuberRegressor (the code's model, defaults) by a batched Newton method with a line search, many problems at once (helper huber_fit). On 240 fits the coefficients differ from sklearn's by at most 1.16e-03 and the withheld R2 by at most 4.4e-05.
Delta R2 refits are run only at electrodes whose full-model R2 exceeds 0.05 in either band (86 models in the main analysis, 84 with the 80/20 split), as every criterion uses Delta R2 only there.
In the code's Delta R2 variant the refit is shared with the Methods' version and the feature is shuffled among the test events before scoring; the code shuffles it over all events before splitting.
The code's log(x + 1) transforms of reach magnitude and onset speed are not run as a variant.

Forward selection runs over design columns (each day and time-of-day one-hot column on its own, as in the code), with the adjusted R2 computed from the rank of the design as statsmodels does. A day or time-of-day feature counts as selected when any of its columns is; the code checks one fixed column. Time-of-day bins are 0-8, 8-16 and 16-24 h without shared edges.

The events are those of reading b of fig2-event-counts (7888), which include the false positives the paper removed, as the files do not mark them; the assumed bad-segment rule and the bad electrodes of each subject's first file are as for fig3-group-lfb-decrease-hfb-increase.

outcomes.notes: Reading a, all 22 good electrodes with LFB R2 > 0.05 and 13 of 14 (0.929) with HFB R2 > 0.05 are assigned to the five frontoparietal regions, and the median R2 of precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal electrodes exceeds that of temporal electrodes in both bands (-0.0097 against -0.0158 in LFB, -0.0117 against -0.0147 in HFB). Reading b, the three regions with the highest projected R2 are precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal in both bands. Few electrodes exceed 0.05, from 4 subjects in LFB and 6 in HFB. These sets overlap the electrodes whose stored R2 (the paper's own, in the files) exceeds 0.05 in 18 electrodes in LFB (22 here, 23 stored, 5 subjects) and 12 in HFB (14 here, 22 stored, 8 subjects). Selected by the stored R2, 22 of 23 LFB and 18 of 22 HFB electrodes are in the five frontoparietal regions (a sensitivity output, not the criterion).
deviations: As for fig6-r2-at-most-025. For reading a an electrode is assigned to the region with its largest weight in the Figshare projection matrix; electrodes whose row is all zero have no region and count as outside the five.

outcomes.notes: Over the 22 good electrodes with LFB R2 > 0.05, reach angle (median Delta R2 0.066) and recording day (0.017) have the two largest median Delta R2; time of day is third (0.0017) and the seven other features have a median of 0. In HFB (14 electrodes) day (0.068) and angle (0.033) are the two largest. The code's Delta R2, the code's selection by LFB R2, the 80/20 split and the inclusion of bad electrodes all give angle and day as the two largest in both bands. Over the electrodes whose stored R2 exceeds 0.05 (23 LFB, 22 HFB; a sensitivity output), angle (0.063) and day (0.013) are the two largest in LFB and day (0.050) and angle (0.019) in HFB, also with the code's Delta R2.
deviations: As for fig6-r2-at-most-025.

outcomes.notes: Angle part holds. Reach angle has the highest projected retention probability in precentral, postcentral and inferior parietal in both bands (0.448 to 0.679, against at most 0.400 for any other feature there). Order part does not hold under either reading. Averaged over the three sensorimotor regions and both bands (reading a) the second to fifth features are onset speed, speech ratio, reach magnitude and bimanual ratio, and over all eight regions (reading b) speech ratio, onset speed, reach magnitude and bimanual ratio; reach duration is sixth and seventh. The second to tenth features lie between 0.202 and 0.357, so the order among them rests on small differences.
deviations: As for fig6-r2-at-most-025. Selection is run once per electrode and band on all of the subject's events, as in the code, so the retention probability of a feature at one electrode is 0 or 1 (a fraction for day and time of day) before projection.

outcomes.notes: The median split-averaged reach-angle coefficient over good electrodes with R2 > 0.05 is -1.027 in LFB (22 electrodes, 0.955 negative) and 0.535 in HFB (14 electrodes, none negative). The code's selection by LFB R2 gives -1.027 and 0.202, the inclusion of bad electrodes -0.815 and 0.515, and the 80/20 split -0.973 and 0.540. By subject, the LFB medians are -1.353 to 0 (4 subjects) and the HFB medians 0 to 0.730 (6 subjects). Over the electrodes whose stored R2 exceeds 0.05 (a sensitivity output), the median is -1.026 in LFB (23 electrodes) and 0.498 in HFB (22).
deviations: As for fig6-r2-at-most-025.

outcomes.notes: Over good electrodes with R2 > 0.05, reach angle and the SD of the day coefficients have the two largest values under both readings and in both bands. LFB angle 1.027 and day 0.660, then time of day 0.188; HFB day 0.733 and angle 0.535, then reach magnitude 0.231 (reading a). The two readings differ only for features whose coefficients change sign. The code's selection by LFB R2, the inclusion of bad electrodes and the 80/20 split give the same two features in both bands and readings. The day SD is the second largest value in LFB and the largest in HFB, which bears on the statement's "large" SD. Over the electrodes whose stored R2 exceeds 0.05 (a sensitivity output), angle and the day SD are also the two largest under both readings in both bands (LFB 1.026 and 0.635, HFB day 0.668 and angle 0.498).
deviations: As for fig6-r2-at-most-025.

The day (and time-of-day) value is the mean over splits of the SD of the one-hot coefficients in each split (helper electrode_model). Taken as the SD of the split-averaged coefficients it is 0.658 against 0.660 in LFB and 0.729 against 0.733 in HFB, and angle and day stay the two largest.

findings.statement: In three files (sub-01 ses-7, sub-04 ses-3, sub-06 ses-3) the ECoG holds 15.5 to 15.9 h and its starting_time is 0, while the reaches table and the pose run on a clock from midnight. The ECoG starts 29241 to 30682 s after midnight, the time missing from 24 h; ReachEvents and the session start time agree, and the movement response appears only with this shift (S06 day 3, precentral HFB +1.98 dB with it, -0.07 dB without). Read with starting_time as given, the event times point at the wrong ECoG or past its end.

The files hold 8088 wrist movement events (211 to 996 per subject), where the data descriptor states 6931 verified events and the paper reports 151 to 947 per subject (median 640). No event is marked as a false positive or as removed, so the events the paper analysed cannot be selected.

Reach_angle_degrees is described only as "Reach angle in degrees". It holds the angle of the reach in image coordinates (y down, -180 to 180), so upward reaches are negative, while the paper's feature is the negated angle folded to -90 to 90.
Pose positions are labelled meters but hold pixels (the data descriptor gives pixels; the values span hundreds).
Bimanual_overlap is described as a fraction of the contralateral movement duration, but 1708 of 8088 values exceed 1 (up to 3.83); it behaves as seconds.
session_start_time is 19:00 at UTC-5 for files that start at local midnight (midnight UTC written in another zone), and 03:07 to 03:31 at UTC-5 for the three files whose ECoG starts later.
124 of the event segments contain missing (NaN) ECoG samples on every electrode, in 30 of 55 files.
The subjects' sex and age, which the paper reports, are not in the files or the archive's metadata.
Seven subjects have electrode groups described as depth in the files (S01, S02, S03, S09, S10, S11, S12), where the paper says five subjects had depth electrodes.
The electrode `good` flags differ between a subject's files, and nothing says which list the paper used; the paper's code takes the list of each subject's first file.

The electrode group descriptions and the data descriptor's Table 2 disagree for two subjects. S11 has groups LATD, LMTD and LTPD described as depth (18 electrodes), where the descriptor gives S11 106 surface and no depth electrodes; S10 has 78 electrodes in groups not described as depth and 48 in depth groups, where the descriptor gives 86 and 40.

The paper's rule for bad ECoG segments ("power <0 dB or with abnormally high power at 115-125 Hz (>3 SDs) compared with all segments") does not say how a segment's power is summarised, in which unit, or whether the SD is over a subject's or all segments, and the preprocessing code is not published. Question for the authors. Was the 0 dB test applied to the log of the mean power density over frequencies and electrodes in microvolts squared, as assumed here? The mean of the log density is below 0 dB for nearly every segment.

The paper does not say how it judged low-frequency decreases "more spatially widespread" than high-frequency increases (Results, Intracortical spectral power, paragraph 2). Question for the authors. Was it the number of regions with significant changes or the extent of significant bins? The two give different answers here.

verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper and the data descriptor. The verifier tested helper functions on synthetic inputs (fold_angle, band and time bins, band_values, segment_power, boot_sig_mask) and checked the archive's asset metadata. It agreed with 19 outcomes and found the six regression claims blocked without good reason.

disagreements.reason: The notebook says "too large", but its own estimate is 3.1 h on one core and 0.8 h on 4 cores, about four times that with the variants, the same order as the 24 min ECoG step it ran. All inputs are in the dataset and already computed in the notebook. None of the six regression claims was tested (B1).

Not run, for the same reason as fig6b-best-models-sensorimotor. The dataset's electrode tables hold the paper's own R2 (max 0.149 LFB, 0.255 HFB), which fits the claim but is the paper's output, not a reproduction.

entries.name: 000055-peterson-2021
entries.title: Behavioral and neural variability of naturalistic arm movements (Peterson et al. 2021)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Peterson, Singh, Wang, Rao and Brunton (2021) on dandiset 000055 (AJILE12), which holds 55 days of ECoG and pose from 12 people in clinical epilepsy monitoring, with their wrist movement events and event features. It compares the behavioural features across subjects and days, the group and per-subject movement-related spectral power in eight cortical regions, the variation of precentral band power across subjects and recording days, and the regression of single-event band power on the behavioural features (Figure 6).

notebooks.title: Reproducing Peterson et al. (2021) from dandiset 000055
